source_text: Ὀναίμην ὑμῶν κατὰ πάντα, ἐάνπερ ἄξιος ὦ. εἰ γὰρ καὶ δέδεμαι, πρὸς ἕνα τῶν λελυμένων ὑμῶν οὐκ εἰμί. οἶδα ὅτι οὐ φυσιοῦσθε: Ἰησοῦν γὰρ Χριστὸν ἔχετε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς: καὶ μᾶλλον, ὅταν ἐπαινῶ ὑμᾶς, οἶδα, ὅτι ἐντρέπεσθε, ὡς γέγραπται, ὅτι ὀ δίκαιος ἑαυτοῦ κατήγορος.
orientation: Ignatius, writing to the Ephesians while a prisoner, has just warned them against empty glory and now turns to his own unworthiness and their humility.
pass_a_gloss: May I have benefit of you in all things, if indeed I am worthy. For if even I have been bound, against one of the loosed ones of you I am not. I know that you are not puffed up: for Jesus Christ you have in yourselves: and rather, whenever I praise you, I know, that you are ashamed, as it has been written, that the righteous one [is] accuser of himself.

choices.english: May I have benefit of you
choices.why: The optative expresses a wish; 'have benefit of' keeps the genitive object and the sense of deriving profit from the Ephesians.
The particle -περ adds emphasis to the condition; 'indeed' preserves that force.

choices.english: of the loosed ones of you
choices.why: The perfect participle λελυμένων contrasts with δέδεμαι ('I have been bound'); 'loosed ones' keeps the verbal force and the contrast.
rejected: of those among you who are free

choices.why: The verb φυσιόω means to be inflated with pride; 'puffed up' is the standard English idiom and matches the metaphor.
The middle voice of ἐντρέπω here means to feel shame or respect; 'you are ashamed' captures the sense of being humbled by praise.

choices.english: the righteous one is accuser of himself
choices.why: The predicate position of κατήγορος with the genitive ἑαυτοῦ is kept literally; the article with δίκαιος marks the class.
rejected: the just one is his own accuser

pass_b_english: May I benefit from you in every way, if indeed I am worthy. For even though I am in chains, I am not equal to one of you who has been set free. I know that you are not puffed up, for you have Jesus Christ within you. And what is more, when I praise you, I know that you are ashamed, as it is written: "The righteous one is his own accuser."

problems.fix: Remove the parenthetical reference or mark as 'unidentified' if no certain source exists.

last_rejected.quote: I am not equal to one of you who has been set free
last_rejected.source_quote: πρὸς ἕνα τῶν λελυμένων ὑμῶν οὐκ εἰμί
last_rejected.why: πρὸς here means 'compared to,' not 'equal to'; Ignatius says he's not even comparable to one freed person among them.
last_rejected.fix: I am not to be compared with even one of you who has been set free.
last_rejected.ruling: πρὸς ἕνα...οὐκ εἰμί naturally conveys 'not equal to one'; rendering captures the comparison adequately.

last_rejected.why: ἐντρέπεσθε means 'you show regard/respect,' not 'you are ashamed'; the sense is modest deference, not shame.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐντρέπεσθε can mean 'ashamed' (LSJ s.v. II); within normal range, not an error.

last_rejected.quote: the righteous one is his own accuser
last_rejected.why: This alludes to Proverbs 18:17 LXX, not a standard citation; but 'accuser' misrepresents the sense. The righteous person is his own examiner/critic, not accuser in a legal sense.
last_rejected.fix: the righteous man is his own critic
last_rejected.ruling: κατήγορος means 'accuser'; rendering is lexically sound. The cited Proverbs 18:17 LXX concern is speculative.
